content:
**Top 5 cancers that cause the most deaths among women worldwide** (According to the most recent GLOBOCAN global cancer‑mortality data – 2020/2021 estimates. The ranking can shift slightly from year to year, but the five cancers below consistently account for the bulk of female cancer deaths worldwide.) | Rank (global female deaths) | Cancer (most common name) | Approx. share of female cancer deaths* | |----------------------------|---------------------------|----------------------------------------| | 1 | **Lung cancer** | ~ 12 % | | 2 | **Breast cancer** | ~ 15 % | | 3 | **Colorectal (colon & rectum) cancer** | ~ 9 % | | 4 | **Stomach (gastric) cancer** | ~ 7 % | | 5 | **Cervical cancer** | ~ 5 % | \*Percentages are rounded; they are drawn from the WHO/IARC GLOBOCAN 2020‑2022 reports, which aggregate incidence and mortality data from > 185 countries. --- ## Typical Symptoms (when they appear) > **Important note** – Most of these cancers are **asymptomatic in early stages**. When symptoms do arise, they can be vague and often overlap with benign conditions. Persistent or worsening signs should prompt a medical evaluation (physical exam, imaging, labs, or appropriate cancer‑screening tests). | Cancer | Common presenting symptoms (ordered by how frequently they are reported) | |--------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------| | **Lung cancer** (most often non‑small‑cell; small‑cell is less common in women) | • Persistent cough or change in a chronic cough
• Shortness of breath (dyspnea)
• Chest pain that may be dull, constant, or worse with deep breathing
• Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) or rust‑colored sputum
• Hoarseness or “brittle” voice (recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement)
• Unexplained weight loss, loss of appetite
• Fatigue or general weakness
• Recurrent infections (e.g., bronchitis, pneumonia)
• Swelling of face or neck (superior vena cava syndrome – rare, late sign) | | **Breast cancer** | • A new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm (most common)
• Change in size, shape, or contour of the breast
• Skin changes: dimpling, puckering, redness, or “peau‑d’orange” (orange‑peel) appearance
• Nipple alterations: inversion, discharge (especially bloody or clear), crusting, or scaling
• Breast pain (usually not the primary symptom, but can accompany)
• Unexplained swelling of the breast
• Persistent itching or rash on the breast skin
• General symptoms (in advanced disease): unexplained weight loss, bone pain (if metastasized), persistent fatigue | | **Colorectal cancer** (colon + rectum) | • Change in bowel habits lasting > 2 weeks (diarrhea, constipation, or alternating)
• Narrowed stool caliber (pencil‑thin stools)
• Blood in stool (bright red or tar‑colored)
• Mucus discharge from the rectum
• Unexplained abdominal cramping or pain (often lower abdomen)
• Unintended weight loss
• Persistent feeling of incomplete evacuation (tenesmus)
• General fatigue or anemia‑related symptoms (pallor, shortness of breath) – often due to chronic occult bleeding | | **Stomach (gastric) cancer** | • Persistent indigestion, heartburn, or “bloating” that does not improve with antacids
• Upper abdominal pain or discomfort (often described as gnawing or burning)
• Unexplained weight loss or loss of appetite
• Early satiety (feeling full after a small amount of food)
• Nausea or vomiting, sometimes with blood (hematemesis)
• Vomiting of coffee‑ground‑like material (digested blood)
• Anemia‑related signs (pallor, fatigue)
• In later stages, palpable abdominal mass, jaundice (if liver involvement) | | **Cervical cancer** | • Abnormal vaginal bleeding (post‑coital bleeding, intermenstrual spotting, or bleeding after menopause)
• Unusual vaginal discharge (watery, mucous‑like, or foul‑smelling)
• Pelvic pain or pain during intercourse (dyspareunia)
• Lower abdominal or pelvic pressure
• Unexplained weight loss or fatigue (often late‑stage)
• In advanced disease, urinary frequency, constipation, or swelling of the legs (due to lymph node involvement) | --- ### Quick “Red‑Flag” Checklist for Women | Symptom | Why it matters | Next step (if you notice it) | |---------|----------------|------------------------------| | Persistent cough or coughing up blood | Could signal lung cancer (or infection) | See a clinician; chest X‑ray/CT and sputum analysis | | New breast lump or nipple changes | Most common early sign of breast cancer | Schedule a clinical breast exam → diagnostic mammogram ± ultrasound/biopsy | | Change in bowel habits + blood in stool | Classic for colorectal cancer | Colonoscopy (screening) or urgent referral if bleeding | | Unexplained weight loss + early satiety | May indicate gastric cancer (or many other malignancies) | Upper‑GI endoscopy (EGD) or imaging (CT abdomen) | | Abnormal vaginal bleeding (especially after sex or menopause) | Early sign of cervical (or endometrial) cancer | Pap smear/HPV testing + pelvic exam; colposcopy if abnormal | --- ## How to Reduce Risk / Catch Early | Cancer | Primary prevention & early‑detection measures | |--------|----------------------------------------------| | Lung | • Smoking cessation (most effective)
• Avoid second‑hand smoke & occupational pollutants
• Low‑dose CT screening for high‑risk women (≥ 55 y, 30 + pack‑years) | | Breast | • Regular mammography (starting age 40‑50, depending on guidelines)
• Clinical breast exam every 1‑2 years (age 20‑39) then annually
• Maintain healthy weight, limit alcohol, stay physically active | | Colorectal | • FIT/FOBT stool‑based test every 1‑2 years (starting age 45)
• Colonoscopy every 10 years (or 5 years if polyps)
• High‑fiber, low‑red‑meat diet; limit alcohol | | Stomach | • Helicobacter pylori eradication where infection is common
• Reduce salt‑preserved foods and smoked foods
• Endoscopic screening in high‑incidence regions (e.g., East Asia) | | Cervical | • HPV vaccination (ideally before sexual debut)
• Pap smear + HPV co‑testing every 3‑5 years (starting age 21)
• Safe sexual practices, smoking cessation | --- ### Bottom line - **Symptoms often appear late**, which is why organized screening programs (mammography, Pap/HPV testing, FIT/colonoscopy, low‑dose CT for smokers) are the most effective way to catch these cancers early and reduce mortality. - If you notice **any persistent, unexplained, or worsening sign** from the tables above, see a healthcare professional promptly. Early evaluation can lead to a definitive diagnosis and, when caught early, dramatically better outcomes.
